clue.text: Temporarily confused "thing" before "item"

indicators.note: a confused set of words is muddled up, so the quoted words and the one between them are jumbled together

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written, though it reads like a positional instruction
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone is briefly muddled over which comes first, a thing or an item.
explanation.walkthrough: 'before' looks like an instruction to place one word ahead of the other, but all fifteen letters of the three words go into the mix.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means for now, until circumstances change, which is what doing something only temporarily implies.

clue.text: Contact boss over publicity he's put first

indicators.note: in a down clue, over means turned upward, so the word for boss is read from the bottom
says the publicity and he's pieces head the answer, ahead of the boss piece

blocks.note: an ad is an advertisement, a piece of publicity
taken as written, apostrophe dropped
the boss is number one, written NO 1, with the digit read as the letter I

explanation.surface: A publicity man insists on being named ahead of the boss whenever someone gets in touch.
explanation.walkthrough: The boss is the number one, and NO 1 is a standard crossword way to write it, the digit standing for the letter I.
explanation.definitionFit: Adhesion is the state of sticking to or touching something, so it is a kind of physical contact.

clue.text: Suggestive of handout covered by revenue

indicators.note: something covered by another thing sits wrapped inside it, so the handout goes within the revenue

blocks.note: rent is the income a landlord earns from property
the dole is state benefit, a handout to the unemployed

explanation.surface: Something hints at a state handout being funded out of rental income.
explanation.walkthrough: The dole is the British name for unemployment benefit.
explanation.definitionFit: Redolent of something means strongly reminding one of it or evoking it, the same as being suggestive of it.

clue.text: Breed fish, relinquishing all rights to visit restaurant?

indicators.note: rights abbreviates to R, and relinquishing all of them means every such letter is given up

blocks.note: to rear animals is to breed them
a trout is a freshwater fish

explanation.surface: A fish farmer abandons their legal rights and goes out for a meal.
explanation.walkthrough: Every R goes, from both words: REAR becomes EA and TROUT becomes TOUT.
explanation.definitionFit: To eat out is to have a meal away from home, typically by going to a restaurant; the question mark marks the loose verb phrase.

clue.text: Courts holding girl about possible output from needles?

indicators.note: about here means turned round, so the girl's name is written backwards
courts holding something keep it inside, so the girl sits within the courting word

blocks.note: to court someone is to woo them
Nell is a girl's name

explanation.surface: A suitor's attentions to a girl are pictured alongside a knitter's work.
explanation.definitionFit: Woollens are knitted garments, and knitting is done with needles, so they are what needles might produce.

clue.text: One in three, otherwise one of two

indicators.note: otherwise means in another way, so the letters of the number are set out differently
one in three puts the single letter inside the reworked number

blocks.note: the Roman numeral for one
taken as written

explanation.surface: It reads like a statement of odds: one chance in three, or else one in two.
explanation.walkthrough: 'otherwise' looks like a link between two halves, but it rearranges THREE, and the I goes inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Either refers to one or the other of a pair, so it names one of two things.

clue.text: Country apartment with no entrance to get through

indicators.note: an entrance is the way in, the front, so the word loses its first letter

blocks.note: a flat is an apartment
via means by way of, through

explanation.surface: A flat with no front door, so getting through is a problem.
explanation.definitionFit: Latvia is a Baltic country in northern Europe, one of the three Baltic states.

clue.text: Composure when modelling perfectly flat cap?

blocks.note: surface reading: a fashion model wearing a flat cap
setter's reading: a cap that sits perfectly flat shows the head beneath is horizontal, not tilted

explanation.surface: A model keeps calm while showing off a flat cap.
explanation.walkthrough: A flat cap is a cloth cap; modelling one perfectly flat means keeping the head exactly even, which is the literal reading of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Being level-headed means staying calm and sensible, which is what composure describes.

clue.text: Uncovered regular 1950s song?

indicators.note: uncovered means stripped of its outer layer, so the word loses its first and last letters

blocks.note: a regular is a professional soldier in a standing army

explanation.surface: A regular customer belts out a song from the 1950s.
explanation.walkthrough: 'regular' looks like an adjective, but it is a noun for a full-time soldier.
explanation.definitionFit: An oldie is an old song still played, and a hit from the 1950s is a typical example, hence the question mark.

clue.text: Detest British rule after a duke absconds

indicators.note: someone who absconds runs off, so that letter leaves the word for rule

blocks.note: taken as written
B is the abbreviation for British
to dominate is to rule over
D is the abbreviation for duke

explanation.surface: People loathe British rule after an aristocrat runs away.
explanation.definitionFit: To abominate is to loathe or regard with intense hatred, the same as to detest.

clue.text: Room let out on a shaky basis?

indicators.note: out suggests the letters are put out of their order, scattered into a new arrangement

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A room is rented out on an insecure, short-term arrangement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'let out' reads as renting a room; only 'out' is the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A tremolo is a wavering, trembling effect in music, so a performance built on it rests on a quivering foundation.

clue.text: Regularly used shore leave to dance in port

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so only every second letter of the next word counts
letters set to dance move about and land in a new order

blocks.note: the second and fourth letters
taken as written

explanation.surface: Sailors spend their shore leave dancing in a harbour town.
explanation.definitionFit: Le Havre is a major French seaport at the mouth of the Seine on the English Channel.

clue.text: Impressive course cut short - one might be shaken by it

definitions.text: one might be shaken by it

indicators.note: something cut short loses its end, so the last letter of the course is dropped

blocks.note: epic means grand or impressive
an entree is a course of a meal

explanation.surface: A grand dinner is curtailed, leaving a diner rattled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'one might be shaken by it' sounds like a nervous guest; it is a place near an earthquake's centre.
explanation.definitionFit: The epicentre is the point on the surface above an earthquake's origin, where the ground and anyone standing there gets shaken hardest.

clue.text: It's sometimes used when smoking fish

blocks.note: first meaning: the filter or butt end of a cannabis joint
second meaning: a freshwater fish of the carp family

explanation.surface: It sounds like a note about the method for smoking fish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'smoking fish' reads as curing fish in smoke; split it, and the smoking part and the fish are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang names the butt or filter of a joint this way, and the same word is a common European freshwater carp species.

clue.text: Fired, say, about hosting fool that's stopped papers

indicators.note: about means turned round, so the abbreviation for say is written backwards
a host has a guest inside, so the fool sits within the turned word
a stopper sits inside a bottle's neck, so this whole group plugs the papers

blocks.note: ID is identification papers
e.g. means for example, as say does
a nit is a fool

explanation.surface: Someone has been sacked for harbouring an idiot who shut down the newspapers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fired' looks like sacked, as the surface has it, but the definition means set alight. Three layers nest here: the fool inside the turned word, and both inside the papers.
explanation.definitionFit: Fired in the sense of set alight or kindled; a fuel that has been ignited has been set burning.

clue.text: Slagging off old dictator in a series of notes

indicators.note: the dictator is placed within the run of musical letters

blocks.note: four consecutive notes of the musical scale
Idi Amin was the dictator of Uganda in the 1970s

explanation.surface: Someone is rubbishing a former dictator in a run of written messages.
explanation.walkthrough: 'notes' look like letters or memos; they are the musical notes D, E, F, G. Slagging off is British slang for criticising harshly.
explanation.definitionFit: Defaming means damaging someone's reputation by false or harsh statements, as slagging them off does.

clue.text: Island, in part, a must-see from the east

indicators.note: in here means contained within the following words, with the answer sitting across them
in an across clue, reading from the east means right to left

blocks.note: letters running across the word boundaries

explanation.surface: A guidebook remarks that part of the island is unmissable for eastern travellers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in part' looks like the hidden signal attached to the island; in fact 'part' is part of the fodder, read backwards from the T of must.
explanation.definitionFit: Sumatra is a large Indonesian island in the western part of the archipelago, west of Java and Borneo.

clue.text: Dickens using US port to abandon maiden number two

indicators.note: to abandon is to leave behind, so that letter is removed from the port
says which of the two matching letters in the port is the one that goes, the second

blocks.note: Memphis, Tennessee, is a river port on the Mississippi
M is the cricket abbreviation for a maiden over
taken as written

explanation.surface: It reads like Charles Dickens sailing from an American port and leaving a second young woman behind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dickens' is not the novelist: 'what the dickens' uses it for the devil. MEMPHIS has two Ms; the second goes, and 'to' stays as written.
explanation.definitionFit: Mephisto, short for Mephistopheles, is the devil of the Faust legend, and dickens is a mild euphemism for the devil.

clue.text: Rag found in middle of ratatouille - cheers

indicators.note: the middle of a word is its central letters, the core around which the rest sits
something found in another is lodged inside it

blocks.note: the three central letters of the eleven
a hanky, a handkerchief, is a piece of cloth like a rag

explanation.surface: A diner finds a scrap of cloth in a vegetable stew and remarks sarcastically on it.
explanation.walkthrough: Cheers is British informal thanks, not only a toast.
explanation.definitionFit: In Britain, cheers is a casual way of expressing gratitude, equivalent to the phrase of thanks.

clue.text: Precise law of old?

blocks.note: ex means former
an act of parliament is a law

explanation.surface: Someone asks for the precise wording of an ancient statute.
explanation.walkthrough: A former law is an ex-act, so the 'of old' piece comes first.
explanation.definitionFit: Exact means accurate in every detail, correct and without error, which is to be precise.

clue.text: Are lass and lad almost striking a pose?

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the last letter of the lad is left off

blocks.note: an are is a metric unit of area, abbreviated A
Kim is a girl's name
a lad is a boy

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a girl and a boy are nearly ready to strike a pose for a photo.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Are' reads as a verb; it is the metric unit of 100 square metres.
explanation.definitionFit: Standing with arms akimbo, hands on hips and elbows out, is a classic posture someone adopts when posing.

clue.text: Climbing rodents and shrew

indicators.note: in a down clue, climbing means going upward, so the letters are read from the bottom

blocks.note: two rats, as the plural asks

explanation.surface: Rats scaling a wall alongside a small mammal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shrew' looks like a third animal, but it means a bad-tempered woman.
explanation.definitionFit: A tartar is a fierce, violent-tempered person, and a shrew is a nagging, ill-tempered woman, so the two are close.

clue.text: Chopped wood put back in hearth

indicators.note: something chopped has been cut off at the end, so the tree loses its last letter

blocks.note: fir is a softwood timber
to replace is to put back

explanation.surface: Freshly chopped logs are returned to the hearth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chopped wood' reads as firewood; only FIR is cut, to FI.
explanation.definitionFit: A fireplace is the recess in a room where a fire burns, and the hearth is the floor of that recess.

clue.text: Withdraw extremely remote flag

indicators.note: extremely points to the extremes of the word, its first and last letters

blocks.note: the first and last letters
to flag is to grow tired, to tire

explanation.surface: Someone retreats to a very far-off place to plant a flag.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flag' looks like a banner; it is the verb meaning to weaken.
explanation.definitionFit: To retire is to retreat or go back from a position, which is to withdraw.

clue.text: Saying English butter must contain stuff

indicators.note: something that must contain another holds it inside, so the stuffing word goes within

blocks.note: E is the abbreviation for English
a ram butts with its head, so it is a butter
to stuff oneself is to pig out

explanation.surface: An old proverb about English butter needing something mixed into it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'butter' is not the dairy spread but an animal that butts with its head; the English letter and that animal together wrap round the stuffing word.
explanation.definitionFit: An epigram is a short, witty remark or pithy statement, which is a kind of saying.

clue.text: Clot takes time, a frantically confused person?

blocks.note: T is the abbreviation for time
such a person is a headless chicken, and a chicken without its head letter is literally that

explanation.surface: An idiot takes a while, being a hopelessly flustered sort.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clot' looks like a noun for a fool; it is the verb, to congeal. Someone panicking is said to run around like a headless chicken; read literally, the chicken loses its C.
explanation.definitionFit: When blood clots it congeals and becomes more solid, which is to thicken.

clue.text: Toff by unopened coach offering piece of cake

indicators.note: unopened means its opening is missing, so the coach loses its first letter

blocks.note: a nob is a toff, a posh upper-class person
a coach trains athletes, a trainer

explanation.surface: A posh man beside a sealed carriage hands over a slice of cake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'coach' reads as a vehicle; it is a sports trainer. A toff is British slang for a rich, upper-class person.
explanation.definitionFit: A no-brainer is a decision or task needing no thought, and a piece of cake is something very easy.

clue.text: The cause of 2 abandoned cars?

indicators.note: abandoned means emptied out, so only the shell of the following word is kept

blocks.note: the digit written as a word
the first and last letters

explanation.surface: A police officer asks what led to two cars being dumped.
explanation.walkthrough: TWOC is British police slang for the offence of Taking WithOut the owner's Consent, joyriding in a stolen car that is then dumped; the whole clue also defines.
explanation.definitionFit: Joyriders who take cars without consent typically dump them afterwards, so such offences cause cars to be left abandoned.
